parsed.modern: The formation of unintractable air in mines cannot be attributed to any variation of atmospheric or there is no natural process with which we are acquainted, by which such a change could be accomplished. In one instance, however, we have an example of a fire-damp being produced, not only without any considerable flagration of atmospheric air, but where there is the belt circulation imaginable. This is in large bellows used in metallurgic works, which are sometimes burst by an explosion of inflammable matter proceeding from the rancid matters with which the leather is greased. Dr Priestley has shown, that inflammable air is composed of pure elementary fire charcoal or phlogiston, and of a little water; and that this composition may take place even in vacuo. All the materials are to be met with in the bowels of the earth. Coal, a bituminous fululence, is abundantly able to supply the phlogiston; the natural motions of the earth affords water, and the heat, however gentle, which constantly exits in the bowels of the earth, may be sufficient to produce a quantity of inflammable air, which gradually accumulating in those places where there is not a constant stream of atmospheric air to carry it off, will soon produce the dreadful effects already mentioned.
